commands.desc: Serve the current directory on port 8000, loopback only
commands.tooltip: Starts Python's built-in static file server on port 8000. The --bind flag restricts it to the loopback interface so only this machine can reach it, which is safer than the default 0.0.0.0 binding that exposes the folder to the local network. Press Ctrl+C to stop.

commands.desc: Serve the dist folder on port 8000
commands.tooltip: Serves a specific folder instead of the current directory, handy for previewing a built SPA before deploying. The --directory flag points the document root at dist while the process runs from anywhere. Add --bind 127.0.0.1 to keep it local only.

commands.desc: Run PHP's built-in dev server with a router script
commands.tooltip: Starts PHP's built-in web server on port 8000, useful for prototyping without configuring Apache or nginx. The second argument names a router script that handles every request, typically by dispatching paths to your front controller. Use -t public to serve a document root instead.

commands.desc: Run PHP's built-in dev server rooted at public
commands.tooltip: Serves the public directory as the document root, the common layout where only public is web-accessible. Requests map to files inside it and index.php is the default entry point. Stop the process with Ctrl+C.

commands.desc: Serve a built SPA on port 3000 with history fallback
commands.tooltip: Serves the build folder on port 3000 with the -s single-page flag, which rewrites unknown paths to index.html so client-side routes work on refresh. npx runs the serve package without a permanent install. Add -C to send permissive CORS headers for local API testing.

commands.desc: Serve a folder over HTTPS with a local certificate
commands.tooltip: Runs serve with TLS using a certificate and key pair, typically generated by mkcert so browsers trust the site without warnings. HTTPS matters when your app uses secure cookies or geolocation. Point a tunnel tool like ngrok at it to test over the public internet.

commands.desc: Serve a folder with the tiny busybox HTTP daemon
commands.tooltip: Serves the public folder on port 8080 using the minimal HTTP daemon bundled with busybox. The -f flag keeps it in the foreground and -p sets the listening port, while -h names the document root. Ideal for containers and embedded systems that lack a full server.

commands.desc: Serve the project on 8080 with caching disabled
commands.tooltip: Serves the current directory on port 8080 with caching turned off, so browser refreshes always fetch fresh files during development. The -c-1 flag sets a negative cache time, which disables the Cache-Control max-age. Pass -o to open the page in a browser automatically.

commands.desc: Start the Vite dev server in the current project
commands.tooltip: Boots Vite's dev server with instant Hot Module Replacement, so edits appear in the browser without a manual reload. It serves source files on port 5173 by default and pre-bundles dependencies for fast startup. Vite reads vite.config.js for custom settings.

commands.desc: Expose the Vite dev server to the local network
commands.tooltip: Starts the dev server bound to 0.0.0.0 instead of localhost, letting phones and other machines on your LAN load the app. Vite prints the network URLs to reach it. Add --port to override the default 5173, or --strictPort to fail instead of switching ports.

commands.desc: Compile the app for production into dist
commands.tooltip: Runs a production build that bundles, minifies and treeshakes your code into the dist folder. The output is static assets you can serve from any host or CDN. Add --sourcemap to emit source maps for debugging minified code.

commands.desc: Build with the staging environment variables
commands.tooltip: Builds the app using the .env.staging environment file, so API URLs and feature flags differ per environment. The --mode flag selects which env file Vite loads alongside the base .env. Run vite build --mode production for the default production output.

commands.desc: Preview the production build locally
commands.tooltip: Serves the dist output with a static server that mimics production behavior, useful to verify the build before deploying. Run vite build first so dist is up to date. This server is for preview only and not hardened for real traffic.

commands.desc: Preview the build on port 4173 for the LAN
commands.tooltip: Serves the built app on port 4173 and exposes it to the local network with --host. Testing the production bundle from a phone catches issues that the dev server masks. Use --strictPort if you want an error instead of a port fallback.

commands.desc: Run the dev script with an extra port argument
commands.tooltip: Executes the dev script from package.json and forwards --port 5173 to it, the standard way to pass arguments through npm. Everything after the double dash reaches the underlying command, such as Vite or Next. Omit the flags to use the port configured in the script.

commands.desc: Restart a Node server automatically on file changes
commands.tooltip: Runs server.js and watches the project, restarting the process whenever a watched file changes. This removes the manual restart cycle during development. Restrict the watch scope with -w src to avoid reloads from logs or build output.

commands.desc: Watch TypeScript files and restart the server
commands.tooltip: Runs a TypeScript server through nodemon while watching ts and tsx extensions for changes. Nodemon itself does not compile TypeScript, so pair it with tsx or ts-node in the exec command. Use -x to override the command nodemon runs.

commands.desc: Run and auto-reload a TypeScript server
commands.tooltip: Executes server.ts with tsx, which compiles TypeScript on the fly through esbuild, and the watch subcommand restarts it on file changes. No separate build step or config file is needed. Ctrl+C stops the watcher.

commands.desc: POST a JSON body with curl's --json shortcut
commands.tooltip: Sends a POST request with the given object as the JSON body and sets Content-Type to application/json automatically. The --json flag is a shorthand for --data with that header, available in curl 7.82 and newer. Add -i to inspect the response headers too.

commands.desc: POST JSON to a local API endpoint
commands.tooltip: Posts a raw JSON payload to your local dev server's API. The -H flag sets the Content-Type header and -d supplies the request body. Use this to exercise endpoints before wiring up the frontend.

commands.desc: Pipe an API response into jq to extract a field
commands.tooltip: Fetches JSON from the API and pipes it to jq, which extracts the id of the first item in the data array. jq makes unstructured JSON responses readable and scriptable. Use -r with jq to print raw strings without quotes.

commands.desc: List every item name from a JSON API response
commands.tooltip: Fetches the API response and jq prints the name of each element in the items array, one per line. The -r flag strips the surrounding quotes for clean output. Swap .items[] for any path that matches your response shape.

commands.desc: Show HTTP status and total time for a request
commands.tooltip: Fetches the page silently and prints a status line with the HTTP status code and total request time. The -w flag formats a write-out message after the transfer, and -s silences the progress bar. Time the pieces with %{time_starttransfer} to isolate server latency.

commands.desc: Measure time to first byte for a request
commands.tooltip: Prints the time until the server starts sending the response body, a proxy for perceived latency. The -o /dev/null flag discards the body and -s hides progress output. Compare this against %{time_total} to see how long the download itself took.

commands.desc: Send a request with HTTP basic auth
commands.tooltip: Adds an Authorization header built from the username and password pair, using HTTP basic authentication. The credentials are base64 encoded, not encrypted, so only use this over HTTPS. For token auth, send an Authorization Bearer header instead.

commands.desc: Send and store cookies across requests
commands.tooltip: Loads cookies from cookies.txt with -b and saves any new ones with -c, simulating a browser session across multiple curl calls. Login first, then reuse the cookie jar for authenticated requests. Use -b 'name=value' to send a single cookie inline.

commands.desc: Follow redirects and accept a self-signed cert
commands.tooltip: Follows redirects with -L and skips TLS certificate verification with -k, useful against dev servers that use self-signed certificates. The -k flag disables a real security check, so avoid it against untrusted hosts. Prefer trusting the certificate with mkcert instead.

commands.desc: Retry a request on transient failures
commands.tooltip: Retries the request up to three times, waiting two seconds between attempts. The --retry-all-errors flag extends retrying beyond timeouts to HTTP-level failures like 5xx responses. Handy for flaky networks in scripts.

commands.desc: Download with a hard timeout to a file
commands.tooltip: Downloads the URL into file.bin and aborts if the transfer takes longer than 10 seconds. The --max-time flag caps the whole operation, unlike --connect-timeout which only bounds the connection phase. Combine with --retry for resilient downloads.

commands.desc: Call an API with a bearer token header
commands.tooltip: Sends a raw Authorization header carrying a bearer token, the standard way to authenticate against modern APIs. Replace TOKEN with the value from your login response. Store it in a shell variable to avoid pasting secrets into history.

commands.desc: Upload a file as multipart form data
commands.tooltip: Posts photo.jpg as a multipart/form-data upload, the same encoding browsers use for file inputs. The @ prefix tells curl to read the file from disk. Add more -F flags for extra fields, like -F 'caption=holiday'.

commands.desc: Send form data with URL encoding
commands.tooltip: Posts a q field containing hello world, with curl percent-encoding the space automatically. The --data-urlencode flag saves you from hand-escaping query values. Use -G instead of -X POST to send encoded fields as a query string.

commands.desc: Build a GET query string with encoded values
commands.tooltip: Sends a GET request whose query string is assembled from the --data-urlencode arguments, so spaces become %20 in the URL. The -G flag switches the data flags from POST body to URL parameters. Repeat the flag for multiple parameters.

commands.desc: Delete a resource with the DELETE method
commands.tooltip: Issues a DELETE request to remove item 42 from the API, the standard way to test destructive endpoints from the terminal. Some servers reply 204 with no body on success. Use --max-time and --retry when scripting deletes against flaky hosts.

commands.desc: Fetch a URL silently but show errors
commands.tooltip: Fetches the page with the progress meter hidden while still printing error messages when the request fails. The -s flag silences progress, and the extra S keeps curl's error output visible. The typical replacement for curl -s in scripts.

commands.desc: Test path traversal without normalizing the URL
commands.tooltip: Sends the literal URL including the ../ segment, because curl otherwise normalizes dot segments before requesting. Use it to probe whether a server leaks files outside the web root. A patched server returns 400 or 404 instead of file contents.

commands.desc: Inspect CORS headers on a response
commands.tooltip: Fetches only the response headers and filters for CORS-related ones like Access-Control-Allow-Origin. The -I flag sends a HEAD request and -s quiets progress output. A missing header here explains why a browser blocks your cross-origin calls.

commands.desc: Check CORS headers with a browser-like Origin
commands.tooltip: Sends a request carrying the Origin header a browser would send from your Vite dev server, then prints the response headers via -D - while discarding the body. Grepping for access-control-allow-origin shows whether the API will permit the call. A wrong value means CORS is misconfigured.

commands.desc: Stream server-sent events from an endpoint
commands.tooltip: Connects to an SSE endpoint and prints each event as it arrives. Server-sent events are a one-way push channel over plain HTTP, unlike WebSockets which are two-way. The -N flag disables buffering so events show up immediately. Press Ctrl+C to disconnect.

commands.cmd: curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"query":"{ user { id } }"}' http://localhost:4000/graphql
commands.desc: Query a GraphQL API with curl
commands.tooltip: Posts a GraphQL query document as JSON to the /graphql endpoint. GraphQL is a query language where clients request exactly the fields they need, and the query string here asks for the id of user. Many servers respond on POST with a JSON body, so pipe it into jq.

commands.desc: Route a request to a local port instead of the DNS host
commands.tooltip: Connects to 127.0.0.1 port 3000 while keeping api.example.com in the URL and TLS certificate checks. This lets you test production-shaped requests against a local server without editing /etc/hosts. The mapping format is host:port:connect-host:connect-port.

commands.desc: Send a Referer header to simulate navigation
commands.tooltip: Sets the Referer header to your dev server origin, mimicking a browser that navigated from the frontend. APIs that validate Referer for CSRF protection or analytics behave as they would for real users. The -e flag stands for referer.

commands.desc: Send a custom User-Agent header
commands.tooltip: Overrides the User-Agent string curl sends by default, useful when a server returns different content to browsers than to scripts. Some APIs reject the default curl agent. Set -A '' to send no User-Agent at all.

commands.desc: Save response headers and body to separate files
commands.tooltip: Writes the response headers to headers.txt with -D and the body to response.json with -o. Splitting them makes it easy to inspect status, cookies and rate-limit headers without burying them in the payload. Add -s to suppress progress noise.

commands.desc: PUT a file as the request body
commands.tooltip: Uploads config.json as the request body using the PUT method, which -T implies without needing -X. This is the classic way to push a file to a REST endpoint. Combine with -H 'Content-Type: application/json' when the API expects JSON.

commands.desc: Read the POST body from a JSON file
commands.tooltip: Sends the contents of payload.json as the request body. The @ prefix makes curl read data from a file instead of the command line, keeping long payloads out of shell history. Add the Content-Type header to match what the server expects.

commands.desc: Throttle a download to test slow networks
commands.tooltip: Downloads the file while capping the transfer rate at 100 kilobytes per second. Simulating a slow connection reveals how your app behaves on mobile networks. The limit applies per transfer, so parallel downloads each get the full rate.

commands.desc: Request a gzip or brotli compressed response
commands.tooltip: Asks the server for a compressed response and decompresses it automatically, saving bandwidth on large pages. curl advertises the encodings it supports in the Accept-Encoding header. Without this flag many servers send uncompressed content.

commands.desc: Fetch a URL with HTTPie's readable output
commands.tooltip: Sends a GET request and prints the response with colorized headers and a highlighted body, far friendlier than raw curl output. HTTPie is a modern curl alternative built for API work. Pipe into jq for further processing.

commands.desc: POST JSON data with HTTPie shorthand
commands.tooltip: Sends a POST with the field name=test converted into a JSON body automatically. Key-value arguments like this are HTTPie's core convenience. Prefix a value with @ to read it from a file, or use := to force a raw JSON value.

commands.desc: Show the full request and response with HTTPie
commands.tooltip: Prints the request line, headers and body alongside the response, the fastest way to debug what exactly is being sent. The -v flag turns on verbose output. Add --print=Hh to show only headers.

commands.desc: Reuse cookies and headers across HTTPie calls
commands.tooltip: Stores cookies and headers from the response into a session named myapi, so later calls with the same session behave like one browser. Login once with --session and every subsequent request carries the auth cookie. Sessions persist in ~/.httpie.

commands.desc: Send a multipart form upload with HTTPie
commands.tooltip: Uploads photo.jpg as a multipart/form-data request, the encoding browsers use for file fields. The -f flag switches HTTPie from JSON to form encoding, and file@ names a file to attach. Add other fields as plain key=value arguments.

commands.desc: Send basic auth credentials with HTTPie
commands.tooltip: Adds an HTTP basic auth header from the username and password pair. The -a flag accepts user:pass or a bare token when combined with -A bearer. Credentials travel base64 encoded, so require HTTPS in production.

commands.desc: Update a resource with HTTPie PUT
commands.tooltip: Sends a PUT request replacing item 42 with the given name field as JSON. PUT semantics replace the whole resource, while PATCH would update only the supplied fields. Use PATCH the same way for partial updates.

commands.desc: Fetch a URL with the fast xh HTTP client
commands.tooltip: Sends a GET request with output styled like HTTPie but implemented in Rust for lower latency and memory use. xh is a drop-in replacement for most HTTPie workflows. Check xh --help for the same key=value argument syntax.

commands.desc: POST JSON data with the xh client
commands.tooltip: Sends a POST request with name=test serialized into a JSON body, mirroring HTTPie's shorthand. xh supports the same field syntax including file@ and := raw values. Use xh --form to switch to form encoding.

commands.desc: Send basic auth with the xh client
commands.tooltip: Adds a basic auth header built from the username and password pair. The -a flag matches HTTPie's auth shorthand, including bearer tokens via -A bearer. All xh flags mirror HTTPie so muscle memory carries over.

commands.desc: Connect to a WebSocket endpoint from the terminal
commands.tooltip: Opens an interactive session against the WebSocket server at localhost:3000, letting you send messages and see replies line by line. A WebSocket is a persistent two-way connection, unlike one-shot HTTP requests. Type Ctrl+D to disconnect.

commands.desc: Connect to a WebSocket in explicit text mode
commands.tooltip: Connects while forcing messages to be sent as WebSocket text frames with the -t flag. This matters when the server distinguishes text from binary messages. Plain websocat already defaults to text, so use -t when you need to be explicit.

commands.desc: Run a WebSocket echo server on port 1234
commands.tooltip: Starts a WebSocket server that echoes back whatever clients send, great for testing WebSocket client code. The -s flag selects server mode with the given port. Connect from another terminal with websocat ws://127.0.0.1:1234/.

commands.desc: Test a WebSocket connection with wscat
commands.tooltip: Connects to a public echo server over a secure WebSocket, where every message you type comes back to you. wscat is the Node.js WebSocket client bundled with the ws library. Press Ctrl+C to close the connection.

commands.desc: Connect to a local WebSocket with an auth header
commands.tooltip: Opens a WebSocket to your local server while sending an Authorization header with the token, matching how your app authenticates sockets. The -H flag repeats for multiple headers. If the handshake fails, check the token and the ws path.

commands.desc: Listen for an incoming WebSocket on port 3000
commands.tooltip: Starts a WebSocket server that accepts a single client and echoes its messages, handy for testing client code without a backend. The -l flag selects listen mode with the port. Messages from the client print on your terminal.

commands.desc: List the gRPC services exposed by a server
commands.tooltip: Queries the server for the services it implements and prints their fully qualified names. The -plaintext flag skips TLS, which most local dev servers expect. gRPC is an RPC framework that serializes calls with protocol buffers, so curl cannot read it directly.

commands.desc: Call a gRPC method with a JSON payload
commands.tooltip: Invokes the SayHello method on the Greeter service, sending the JSON message which grpcurl converts to the binary protobuf format. The -d flag supplies the request body and method names use the service slash method syntax. Omit -d to send an empty message.

commands.desc: List services from proto files without reflection
commands.tooltip: Reads the service definitions from your local proto files when the server has reflection disabled. The -import-path flag points at the directory containing the schemas and -proto names the file to load. The same flags work with describe to inspect messages.

commands.desc: Show the methods and types of a gRPC service
commands.tooltip: Prints the full definition of the Greeter service, including every method signature and its request and response types. describe works from server reflection or from -proto files. It is the fastest way to learn an unfamiliar API's contract.

commands.desc: Generate JavaScript code from a proto file
commands.tooltip: Runs the protocol buffer compiler to emit JavaScript modules from user.proto into the current directory. The --js_out flag takes options like import_style=commonjs and the output directory after the colon. The generated files work with the google-protobuf runtime.

commands.desc: Generate Go code and gRPC stubs from a proto
commands.tooltip: Compiles service.proto into Go structs in the current directory plus the gRPC client and server interfaces. The --go_out flag generates message types and --go-grpc_out generates the service code. Run protoc --version to confirm the compiler is installed.

commands.desc: Lint your proto files for style violations
commands.tooltip: Checks the protobuf files in the current directory against Buf's style rules, catching naming and compatibility problems before codegen. Buf is the modern build tool for protocol buffers. Configure rules in buf.yaml at the repo root.

commands.desc: Generate code from protos using buf
commands.tooltip: Runs code generation for every language configured in buf.gen.yaml, replacing hand-written protoc invocations. Buf manages plugins and import paths automatically. Add buf lint before it in CI to catch issues early.

commands.desc: Load test with ApacheBench at 50 concurrent
commands.tooltip: Sends 1000 requests with 50 running concurrently, reporting requests per second and latency percentiles. ApacheBench ships with the apache2-utils package and needs no config file. It is single-URL only, so use wrk or k6 for complex scenarios.

commands.desc: Load test with keep-alive connections
commands.tooltip: Runs 5000 requests at 100 concurrency while reusing connections with the -k flag. Keep-alive models real browser behavior and shows higher throughput than fresh connections per request. Compare both runs to see connection setup overhead.

commands.desc: Load test an authenticated endpoint
commands.tooltip: Sends 100 requests with a bearer token header on every one, exercising routes that require login. The -H flag repeats for additional headers. Watch the non-2xx count in the report to confirm auth is not failing under load.

commands.desc: Load test with wrk using 4 threads and 100 connections
commands.tooltip: Runs a 30 second benchmark with 4 threads sharing 100 connections, reporting requests per second and latency. wrk keeps a persistent connection per thread, so results reflect keep-alive behavior. Threads and connections are separate knobs: raise -c for more concurrency.

commands.desc: Load test with a latency histogram
commands.tooltip: Runs a 10 second test and prints a detailed latency distribution with the --latency flag. The histogram shows percentiles like 75% and 99%, revealing tail latency that averages hide. Short runs with high variance warrant a longer -d duration.

commands.desc: Load test with hey at 10000 requests
commands.tooltip: Fires 10000 requests with 100 workers and prints a summary with latency histograms and status code counts. hey is a Go load generator that supports custom methods, headers and bodies. Add -z 30s to switch from request counts to a time window.

commands.desc: Load test for a fixed duration with hey
commands.tooltip: Sends requests for 30 seconds with 50 workers, which is easier to reason about than a fixed request count. The -z flag sets the duration and -m overrides the HTTP method. Add -d to supply a request body for POST tests.

commands.desc: Stress a URL with 50 simulated users for 60 seconds
commands.tooltip: Simulates 50 concurrent users hitting the URL for 60 seconds and reports transactions, response times and availability. The -c flag sets concurrency and -t sets the run time. Point siege at a urls.txt file with -f to spread load across many pages.

commands.desc: Benchmark with autocannon at 50 connections
commands.tooltip: Runs a 20 second benchmark with 50 concurrent connections and prints a rich table of latency percentiles and request rates. autocannon is a Node.js load tester that supports pipelining and warmup phases. Add -a to cap total requests instead of duration.

commands.desc: Run a k6 load test script
commands.tooltip: Executes the JavaScript load test in script.js, which defines virtual users, scenarios and thresholds. k6 compiles the script with its own JS runtime and reports rich metrics. Set thresholds in the script to make the run pass or fail like a unit test.

commands.desc: Run k6 with 100 virtual users for 30 seconds
commands.tooltip: Overrides the script's load profile with 100 virtual users running for 30 seconds. A virtual user is one simulated user executing the test scenario. CLI flags take precedence over options declared in the script.

commands.desc: Run k6 for a fixed number of iterations
commands.tooltip: Runs 1000 total iterations shared across 10 virtual users, useful when you want a deterministic amount of work rather than a time window. Each iteration executes the default exported function once. Combine with --duration to bound the run.

commands.desc: Export k6 results to a JSON file
commands.tooltip: Runs the test and streams metrics into results.json for later analysis or graphing. The --out flag accepts named outputs like json, csv and experimental-prometheus-rw. Point several outputs at once by repeating the flag.

commands.desc: Log every HTTP request and response in k6
commands.tooltip: Prints the full request and response details for each HTTP call the test makes, invaluable for debugging flaky scripts. The --http-debug flag takes values like headers or full, where full includes bodies. Expect very noisy output, so scope runs tightly.

commands.desc: Skip TLS verification in k6 against dev servers
commands.tooltip: Disables certificate validation for the test run, needed when load testing local servers that use self-signed certificates. This mirrors curl -k and weakens security, so never use it against production hosts. Prefer mkcert-issued certificates instead.

commands.desc: Attack a URL list and report results in one pipe
commands.tooltip: Sends requests to every URL listed in urls.txt at 100 requests per second for 30 seconds, piping the binary results straight into the text report. Vegeta's attack output is a binary stream meant for other vegeta commands. Save it with -output for later analysis.

commands.desc: Save raw vegeta attack results to a file
commands.tooltip: Runs the attack and writes the binary result stream to results.bin instead of stdout. Keeping the raw data lets you regenerate any report later. Feed the file into vegeta report, plot or encode without rerunning the load.

commands.desc: Report vegeta results as a latency histogram
commands.tooltip: Prints how many requests fell into each latency bucket defined inside the brackets. Histogram reports reveal response time distributions that averages hide. The bucket list is comma separated and measured in milliseconds.

commands.desc: Generate an interactive HTML chart from vegeta results
commands.tooltip: Renders the attack results as a self-contained HTML page with latency and throughput charts. Open plot.html in any browser to inspect the run visually. The output goes to stdout, so the redirect writes the file.

commands.desc: Convert vegeta binary results to CSV
commands.tooltip: Decodes the binary attack results from stdin into CSV rows with timestamp, status and latency columns. The -to flag selects the output encoding among csv, gob and json. Feed the CSV into spreadsheets or pandas for custom analysis.

commands.desc: Run a locust load test headlessly
commands.tooltip: Executes the load test defined in locustfile.py with 100 simulated users spawning at 10 per second, for 60 seconds. The --headless flag skips the web UI and prints results to the terminal. Press Ctrl+C early to stop and see partial metrics.

commands.desc: Install the Chromium browser for Playwright
commands.tooltip: Downloads the Chromium build pinned to your Playwright version into the browser cache. Playwright tests fail with a clear message when the browser is missing. Add --with-deps to install the system libraries the browser needs.

commands.desc: Install Chromium plus its system dependencies
commands.tooltip: Installs Chromium and uses apt to fetch the operating system libraries it requires, handy on fresh CI images and containers. The --with-deps flag needs sudo on some setups. Run it once per machine or CI image.

commands.desc: Run the Playwright test suite
commands.tooltip: Executes every test file matching the default pattern, running browsers headlessly and reporting failures with traces. Tests live in files like tests/example.spec.js. Add --headed to watch them run in a visible browser.

commands.desc: Run Playwright tests in a visible browser
commands.tooltip: Runs the suite with browsers shown on screen instead of headless, useful for debugging flaky selectors and watching the app behave. Combined with --debug you get the inspector and step controls. Keep headless for CI runs.

commands.desc: Run only tests matching a name pattern
commands.tooltip: Filters the suite to tests whose titles contain login, using the -g grep flag. The pattern is a regular expression, so 'checkout|payment' matches either term. Speeds up iteration when only one flow changed.

commands.desc: Run tests for a single browser project
commands.tooltip: Restricts the run to the chromium project defined in playwright.config.js, skipping firefox and webkit. Projects let one suite target multiple browsers with different viewports. Use --project=firefox to compare cross-browser behavior.

commands.desc: Record browser actions as Playwright code
commands.tooltip: Opens a browser window where every click and keystroke is converted into Playwright test code in real time. The generated script is a solid starting point for a new test. Add -o test.spec.js to save it straight to a file.

commands.desc: Capture a full-page screenshot with Playwright
commands.tooltip: Renders the page in a headless browser and saves a screenshot spanning the entire scrollable height, not just the viewport. The --full-page flag captures everything below the fold. Add --device 'iPhone 13' to emulate a phone viewport.

commands.desc: Screenshot a site as a mobile device
commands.tooltip: Emulates an iPhone 13 viewport and touch behavior while capturing the full page, revealing mobile layout issues without a physical device. The --device flag accepts names from Playwright's device registry. Combine with --wait-for-timeout to let lazy content load.

commands.desc: Open a URL in a Playwright-controlled browser
commands.tooltip: Launches a browser window driven by Playwright, handy for quick manual exploration with the inspector. It behaves like a clean automation browser with no extensions or profile. Add --device to emulate a specific device.

commands.desc: Open the last Playwright HTML test report
commands.tooltip: Serves and opens the HTML report from the last test run, with retries, traces and per-test video. The report lives in playwright-report by default. Pass a path argument to view a different report directory.

commands.desc: Inspect a Playwright trace recording
commands.tooltip: Opens the trace viewer for trace.zip, showing every action, network request and console message from a failed test. Traces are recorded automatically on test failure. They are the fastest way to diagnose flaky end-to-end tests.

commands.desc: Audit a page and save the report as JSON
commands.tooltip: Runs Lighthouse audits for performance, accessibility and best practices, writing the machine-readable JSON report to lh.json. The --output flag selects the format and --output-path names the file. Parse the JSON in CI to enforce score budgets.

commands.desc: Audit only performance and accessibility
commands.tooltip: Limits the audit to the listed categories, cutting run time and focusing the report. Categories include performance, accessibility, best-practices and seo. Combine with --output=html --output-path to keep a browsable report.

commands.desc: Audit a local dev site and open the report
commands.tooltip: Runs Lighthouse against your local server and opens the HTML report in the browser with --view. Testing localhost catches performance regressions before they ship. Note that local machines often score differently than production hardware.

commands.desc: Audit with the desktop preset and save HTML
commands.tooltip: Runs the audit using desktop emulation settings instead of the mobile defaults, matching how Lighthouse scores desktop sites. The --preset flag accepts perf, experimental and desktop. The HTML report opens in any browser for sharing.

commands.desc: Audit headlessly with custom Chrome flags
commands.tooltip: Passes flags to the Chrome instance Lighthouse launches, like --no-sandbox for containers, and suppresses progress output with --quiet. The --chrome-flags value is space delimited inside the quotes. Useful in CI environments without a display.

commands.desc: Run the Cypress test suite headlessly
commands.tooltip: Executes all end-to-end tests in headless mode and prints a summary with per-spec results. Cypress runs in the browser and captures screenshots and video on failure. Add --browser chrome to pick a specific browser.

commands.desc: Open the Cypress interactive test runner
commands.tooltip: Launches the Cypress app where you can pick a spec file and watch tests run live, with time travel debugging and network inspection. Changes to specs reload automatically. The first run creates the cypress folder structure.

commands.desc: Run a single Cypress spec file
commands.tooltip: Executes only the login spec instead of the whole suite, shortening iteration cycles. The --spec flag accepts glob patterns too, like cypress/e2e/*.cy.js. Add --headed to watch the run in a visible browser.

commands.desc: Create and trust a local certificate authority
commands.tooltip: Generates a local CA, installs it into the system trust store and registers it with Firefox and Chrome. Browsers then trust certificates that mkcert signs, killing self-signed warning screens. The CA key grants full TLS interception power, so never share it.

commands.desc: Issue a locally trusted cert for localhost
commands.tooltip: Creates a certificate valid for both localhost and the loopback IP, written to the named files. The names listed after the flags become the certificate's subject alternative names. Point your dev server at cert.pem and key.pem to serve trusted HTTPS.

commands.desc: Issue a cert covering localhost and a domain
commands.tooltip: Generates a certificate valid for both localhost and example.com, handy when an app is reachable through a tunnel or hosts file entry. mkcert names the output files after the domains, like localhost+1.pem. Add '*.example.com' to cover subdomains.

commands.desc: Issue a cert with a wildcard domain
commands.tooltip: Creates a certificate covering example.com and any subdomain, matching how production wildcard certs behave. Quote the wildcard so the shell does not expand it. Great for testing cookie scoping and multi-subdomain setups locally.

commands.desc: Print the local CA certificate directory
commands.tooltip: Shows where mkcert stores rootCA.pem and rootCA-key.pem. Copy rootCA.pem to phones or containers to trust the same CA there, or point NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS at it for Node.js. Keep the key file private.

commands.desc: Remove the local CA from trust stores
commands.tooltip: Deletes the local CA from the system and browser trust stores, so mkcert-signed certificates stop being trusted. Certificates already issued remain valid until they expire but will show warnings again. The CA files themselves stay on disk until you delete them.

commands.desc: Generate a self-signed cert with SANs
commands.tooltip: Creates a 2048-bit RSA key and a self-signed certificate valid for a year, with the subject alternative names that modern browsers require. The -nodes flag keeps the key unencrypted so servers can load it without a passphrase. Browsers still warn because no trusted CA signed it.

commands.desc: Inspect the TLS certificate a dev server presents
commands.tooltip: Connects to the TLS listener on port 3000 and prints the full certificate chain, cipher and handshake details. The -showcerts flag dumps every certificate in the chain. Use it to debug why a local HTTPS server looks wrong. The command waits on stdin, so pipe echo to it.

commands.desc: Map a fake domain to localhost in /etc/hosts
commands.tooltip: Appends a hosts entry pointing myapp.local at the loopback address, so the domain resolves without DNS. Web apps often require real-looking hostnames for cookies and CORS. Use sudo tee because /etc/hosts needs root, and remove the line when done.

commands.desc: Override a service unit with a drop-in file
commands.tooltip: Opens an editor for a systemd drop-in that layers settings over the postgresql service without editing the package unit. Changes like environment overrides or resource limits go in the override.conf file. Save and run sudo systemctl restart postgresql to apply.

commands.desc: Run a throwaway Postgres 16 container for dev
commands.tooltip: Starts Postgres 16 in a detached container named dev-postgres, with the password env var set and port 5432 published. The -d flag daemonizes it and -p maps the port. Connect with psql -h localhost -U postgres, and remove the container with docker rm -f dev-postgres when done.

commands.desc: Run a Redis 7 container for local development
commands.tooltip: Launches a slim Redis instance in a detached container mapped to port 6379. The alpine variant keeps the image small for dev machines. Use redis-cli -p 6379 PING to verify it responds, then docker stop dev-redis when finished.

commands.cmd: docker compose exec db psql -U app appdb -c 'SELECT 1'
commands.desc: Run psql inside the compose database service
commands.tooltip: Executes a query inside the running db service container without opening a shell first. The -c flag passes the SQL directly, and -U selects the app user against the appdb database. A 1 in the result confirms the database is healthy.

commands.desc: Approve an .envrc file for direnv to load
commands.tooltip: Grants direnv permission to evaluate the .envrc file in the current directory, which exports project-specific environment variables whenever you enter it. The security gate exists so cloned repos cannot run arbitrary code silently. Re-run after editing the file, or use direnv edit to reload automatically.

commands.desc: Edit the .envrc file and reload it
commands.tooltip: Opens .envrc in your editor and marks it allowed afterwards, skipping the separate allow step. direnv watches the file and loads the new environment on the next prompt. Combine with direnv status to debug why variables are missing.

commands.desc: Force direnv to reload the current environment
commands.tooltip: Re-evaluates the current directory's .envrc immediately instead of waiting for the next prompt. Useful after changing direnv itself or the stdlib. Run direnv status first if variables look stale.

commands.desc: Revoke permission for the current .envrc
commands.tooltip: Blocks the .envrc in the current directory so direnv refuses to load it, undoing a previous allow. The file still exists on disk, only the permission is revoked. Re-allow it later if you change your mind.

commands.desc: Show direnv diagnostics and state
commands.tooltip: Prints the direnv version, loaded environment diff and which .envrc files are allowed, the first stop when the environment misbehaves. It also shows the shell hook status. The output is verbose but reveals stale or conflicting exports.

commands.desc: Run a command with the directory's env loaded
commands.tooltip: Executes npm run dev with the environment from the current directory's .envrc, without relying on the shell hook or an interactive session. Ideal for scripts and editors that do not trigger direnv. The first argument is the directory, the rest is the command.

commands.desc: Load .env variables into the current shell
commands.tooltip: Reads .env, skips comment lines and exports every KEY=value pair into the current shell session. The command substitution runs grep and xargs, whose output becomes the export arguments. Values with spaces break the parsing, so prefer direnv for complex files.

commands.desc: Run the default recipe from the justfile
commands.tooltip: Executes the first recipe in the project's justfile, conventionally named default, which often prints help or runs the main workflow. just is a command runner that stores project commands as recipes. List them with just -l.

commands.desc: List all recipes in the justfile
commands.tooltip: Prints every recipe name together with the comment above it, serving as built-in documentation. The -l flag is short for --list. Hidden recipes starting with an underscore are omitted.

commands.desc: Run the build recipe from the justfile
commands.tooltip: Executes the recipe named build, which typically compiles, bundles or packages the project. Recipes are defined in the justfile and run in a shell. Pass arguments after the recipe name when it declares parameters.

commands.desc: Show what a recipe would run without executing
commands.tooltip: Prints every command that the build recipe would execute, without running any of them. The --dry-run flag is perfect for auditing a recipe before trusting it, or copying the exact commands into CI. Combine with -v for more detail.

commands.desc: Print the value of a justfile variable
commands.tooltip: Evaluates the VERSION variable defined in the justfile and prints its value, useful for scripting and debugging. Without an argument, --evaluate dumps every variable. Variables are evaluated in the justfile's directory context.

commands.desc: Print the fully resolved justfile
commands.tooltip: Outputs the justfile after all modules and imports are combined, showing the effective configuration. The --dump flag helps trace where a recipe or variable came from. Pipe it to a file to compare with the source.

commands.desc: List tasks defined in the Taskfile
commands.tooltip: Prints every task from Taskfile.yml with its description, the fastest way to discover a project's commands. The -l flag is short for --list. Add --json for machine-readable output.

commands.desc: Run the build task from the Taskfile
commands.tooltip: Executes the task named build, which can run shell commands, depend on other tasks and pass environment variables. Task is a Make-inspired runner written in Go. Use task --init to create a starter Taskfile.

commands.desc: Re-run a task whenever files change
commands.tooltip: Runs the build task and watches the project, re-executing it on every file change. The --watch flag defaults to a 5 second poll interval, tunable with --interval. Perfect for rebuild-on-save loops.

commands.desc: Show detailed info about a task
commands.tooltip: Prints the task's full definition including its commands, dependencies and variables without running anything. The --summary flag complements --list, which only shows one-line descriptions. Combine with --status to check freshness.

commands.desc: Create a starter Taskfile in the current directory
commands.tooltip: Writes a Taskfile.yml with example tasks and the schema version header. The file is a safe starting point for converting ad-hoc scripts into named tasks. Edit it and run task -l to see your tasks listed.

commands.desc: Expose this machine to VS Code over a secure tunnel
commands.tooltip: Starts the VS Code CLI tunnel, making the machine reachable from vscode.dev or any VS Code client through Microsoft's tunnel service. No SSH or public IP is needed. It prints a vscode.dev URL after authenticating with GitHub or Microsoft.

commands.desc: Start a VS Code tunnel with a fixed name
commands.tooltip: Names the tunnel mytunnel so the same machine is always identifiable across sessions instead of getting a random name. Stable names matter when you connect from several clients. Run code tunnel unregister to remove a machine.

commands.desc: Open a project on a remote host in VS Code
commands.tooltip: Launches VS Code connected over SSH to myserver, opening /path/to/project on that machine with extensions and terminal running remotely. The ssh-remote+ prefix selects the SSH transport, and the host must exist in your SSH config. The Remote-SSH extension handles the connection.

commands.desc: Build and start the dev container for this project
commands.tooltip: Reads .devcontainer/devcontainer.json and creates or starts the development container for the current folder, installing features and mounting the workspace. The CLI variant of VS Code's Reopen in Container. Run it before devcontainer exec to interact with the environment.

commands.desc: Open a shell inside the running dev container
commands.tooltip: Runs bash inside the container created for the current workspace, giving you the project's toolchain without leaving the terminal. The --workspace-folder flag selects which container. Useful for running builds and tests from scripts.

commands.desc: Build the dev container image without starting it
commands.tooltip: Builds the image defined by the devcontainer.json configuration and stops there, without creating a container. Pre-building images speeds up later starts and validates the Dockerfile. Add --image-name to tag the result.

commands.desc: Search only JavaScript files with ripgrep
commands.tooltip: Finds pattern in files matching the *.js glob, skipping everything else. The -g flag filters by glob and can be repeated, with an exclamation-mark prefix to exclude, like -g '!*.test.js'. ripgrep is the fast, gitignore-aware successor to grep.

commands.desc: List project files excluding node_modules
commands.tooltip: Prints every file tracked in the project, honoring .gitignore and skipping node_modules. The --files mode turns ripgrep into a fast file lister. Use it to feed other tools like xargs without the noise of dependencies.

commands.desc: Find TODO and FIXME comments in source
commands.tooltip: Searches the src directory for TODO or FIXME markers and prints each hit with its line number thanks to -n. The pattern is a regular expression, so the vertical bar means or. Add --type js to scope by language.

commands.desc: Count lines of every markdown file
commands.tooltip: Finds all md files and runs wc -l on each one, printing their line counts. The -e flag filters by extension and -x executes a command per result, appending the file path. fd is a fast, intuitive replacement for find.

commands.desc: List directories up to two levels deep
commands.tooltip: Shows only directories with the -t d type filter, limited to two levels of nesting by --max-depth. The compact output makes it easy to map a project's structure. Add -H to include hidden directories like .git.

commands.desc: Pick a file with a syntax-highlighted preview
commands.tooltip: Opens the fuzzy finder where typing filters results and the preview pane renders the highlighted file with bat. The {} placeholder is replaced by the selected line. Use --multi to select several entries with Tab.

commands.desc: Select multiple items in the fuzzy finder
commands.tooltip: Enables Tab-based multi-selection in fzf, printing all chosen lines when you press Enter. Combine with a preview flag to inspect each candidate. Pipe the output into xargs for batch operations.

commands.desc: Show only the changed lines of a file
commands.tooltip: Displays file.js with just the lines added, removed or modified versus the git index, styled like a diff. The --diff flag highlights the changes bat detects in the repository. Pipe the file in to diff against anything else.

commands.desc: View a file with an explicit language theme
commands.tooltip: Renders package.json with JSON syntax highlighting, overriding bat's auto-detection. The -l flag forces the language, handy for extensionless or misdetected files. Combine with --line-range 1:20 to view a slice.

commands.desc: Add a directory to the zoxide database
commands.tooltip: Records the projects/myapp path so the z command can jump to it later by name. zoxide ranks directories by how often you use them. Run this once for paths outside your shell history.

commands.desc: Look up the best match for a directory name
commands.tooltip: Prints the highest-ranked path matching myapp from the zoxide database, without changing directory. The query command is what the z alias calls under the hood. Add -i for an interactive picker.

commands.desc: Generate the zoxide shell hook for bash
commands.tooltip: Emits the shell configuration that wires the z and zi commands into bash, with completion support. Wrap it in eval, like eval "$(zoxide init bash)", inside .bashrc. Pick zsh or fish to match your shell.

commands.desc: Proxy port 8080 to localhost:3000 with verbose logs
commands.tooltip: Forwards every connection on port 8080 to the server on port 3000, with -v printing a readable dump of the data flowing both ways. The fork option handles each new connection separately. This exposes what a client actually sends to your app.

commands.desc: Intercept HTTP traffic through a web UI
commands.tooltip: Starts a man-in-the-middle proxy on port 8080 with a browser UI on port 8081 for inspecting and editing requests and responses. Point curl or a browser at the proxy with -x http://localhost:8080. Install mitmproxy's CA certificate to decrypt HTTPS traffic.

commands.desc: Capture proxy traffic to a file non-interactively
commands.tooltip: Runs the command-line mitmproxy without a UI, dumping every intercepted flow into flows.mitm. Replay or inspect the capture later with mitmweb -r flows.mitm. Script it with Python addons for automated request rewriting.

commands.desc: Capture raw HTTP traffic on the loopback interface
commands.tooltip: Prints every packet on the loopback interface for port 3000, with -A showing the payload as ASCII so HTTP headers are readable. Loopback traffic often escapes normal sniffing tools, making this the way to see exact bytes. Needs root for packet capture.

commands.desc: Forward a local port to a remote service
commands.tooltip: Creates a secure tunnel so localhost:3000 on your machine forwards to port 3000 on the staging host. The -L flag maps local port to remote host and port. This reaches services that are not exposed publicly, like a database admin UI.

commands.desc: Expose a local port on a remote server
commands.tooltip: Publishes your local port 3000 as port 9000 on the remote host, letting others reach your dev server through it. The -R flag reverses the normal forward direction. Pair with a reverse proxy on the remote box for a public URL.

commands.desc: Expose the local dev server via a public URL
commands.tooltip: Creates a public HTTPS URL that tunnels into your local port 3000, so clients anywhere can hit your dev server. ngrok prints the assigned URL and a web inspection dashboard. Add --url with a reserved domain for a stable address.

commands.desc: Tunnel to a fixed ngrok domain
commands.tooltip: Serves your local port 8080 through the reserved domain myapp.ngrok.app, keeping the URL stable across restarts. Fixed domains matter for OAuth callbacks and webhook configuration. Reserve the domain first in the ngrok dashboard.

commands.desc: List the tables in a SQLite dev database
commands.tooltip: Prints every table name stored in dev.db, the fastest orientation when opening an unfamiliar database. The dot command runs inside the sqlite3 shell. Use .schema users to see a table's columns and indexes.

commands.desc: Query SQLite with aligned column output
commands.tooltip: Runs the query and formats the result as aligned columns with a header row, instead of the pipe-separated default. The -header and -column flags are command-line equivalents of the .headers and .mode dot commands. Append ; to end the SQL statement.

commands.desc: Create and apply the first Prisma migration
commands.tooltip: Compares your Prisma schema with the database, generates a migration named init and applies it, then regenerates the client. The dev subcommand is for local databases and can be destructive with reset. Review the generated SQL in prisma/migrations before committing.

commands.desc: Regenerate the Prisma Client from the schema
commands.tooltip: Recreates the type-safe Prisma Client in node_modules from your schema.prisma, required after schema changes. The generated client gives autocompletion and compile-time checks. Run it after every prisma migrate or db push.

commands.desc: Browse and edit data with Prisma Studio
commands.tooltip: Launches a browser-based data explorer at localhost:5555 for inspecting and editing records through your Prisma models. Studio connects to the database URL in your schema. Close it with Ctrl+C when done.

commands.desc: Sync the schema to the database without migrations
commands.tooltip: Pushes your Prisma schema directly to the database, creating tables and columns without generating migration files. Best for early prototyping when history does not matter. Switch to prisma migrate dev once the schema stabilizes.

commands.desc: Apply pending migrations in production
commands.tooltip: Runs every migration in prisma/migrations that has not been applied yet, the safe command for staging and production. Unlike migrate dev it never resets data or prompts. Pair it with prisma generate afterwards to refresh the client.

commands.desc: Mock a REST API from a JSON file
commands.tooltip: Serves db.json as a full REST API with GET, POST, PUT and DELETE routes generated from its top-level keys, on port 4000. json-server is the fastest way to fake a backend while the real one is built. Point the frontend at it with a proxy or env var.

commands.desc: Serve static files alongside the mock API
commands.tooltip: Serves the public folder as static assets on the same origin as the fake REST API, so the frontend and API share a port. The --static flag sets that directory. Combined with --port you get a complete local app.

commands.desc: Lint an OpenAPI spec for errors and style
commands.tooltip: Validates openapi.yaml against the OpenAPI ruleset, reporting broken references, missing fields and naming problems. The lint command exits non-zero on errors, so it slots into CI. Auto-fix simple issues with the --format option and redocly lint --extends recommended.

commands.desc: Merge a multi-file OpenAPI spec into one file
commands.tooltip: Resolves all $ref includes and bundles the spec into a single document on stdout, ready for tools that need one file. The bundle command is the glue step before publishing docs or generating clients. Redirect output to a file to keep it.

commands.desc: Read a value from a YAML file with yq
commands.tooltip: Prints the image key under services.db, using the same dot-path syntax as jq but for YAML. yq is the standard YAML processor for scripts and CI. Use -i with an assignment to edit files in place.

commands.desc: Edit a YAML value in place with yq
commands.tooltip: Rewrites docker-compose.yml setting the api service ports list, with -i saving changes back to the file. The expression uses jq-style assignment syntax. Back up the file first since in-place edits are irreversible.

commands.desc: Kill the process listening on port 3000
commands.tooltip: Terminates whatever process holds the TCP port 3000, the classic fix for address already in use errors. The -k flag sends SIGKILL after locating the owner. Check with fuser 3000/tcp first, since the kill is immediate and unconfirmed.

commands.desc: Show which process is using port 3000
commands.tooltip: Lists the process holding port 3000, including its PID and command name. lsof is the standard answer to which process stole my port. Add -P to skip name resolution for faster output.

commands.desc: Run tests automatically when files change
commands.tooltip: Watches every js file in src and reruns npm test whenever one changes, with -r restarting the process each time. entr is a minimal file-watcher that runs a command on stdin changes. Press Ctrl+D to stop watching.

commands.desc: Run a Node server as a managed daemon
commands.tooltip: Starts server.js as a background process named api, restarted automatically if it crashes and saved across reboots with pm2 save. PM2 is a process manager aimed at Node services. Watch logs with pm2 logs api.

commands.desc: Stream logs from a PM2-managed process
commands.tooltip: Follows stdout and stderr of the api process in real time, with timestamps and line wrapping. The logs flag tails combined output for all processes when no name is given. Press Ctrl+C to stop following without stopping the app.

commands.desc: Restart a PM2 process by name
commands.tooltip: Cycles the api process, reloading its code after a deploy or config change. Restart is graceful by default, draining in-flight requests when using the cluster mode. List all processes with pm2 ls.
